entries.question: What is the shape of the earth?
entries.summary: Isaiah 40:22 describes God sitting upon the "circle of the earth," which apologists routinely cite as evidence the Bible knew the planet was spherical. Matthew 4:8 then has the devil taking Jesus up a mountain high enough to see "all the kingdoms of the world" — a geometry that only works on a flat earth. The contradiction is between a text apologists read as scientifically prescient and a text that assumes a flat-earth cosmology where altitude provides global visibility.
entries.commentary: First the Isaiah verse, because the apologetic case rests entirely on a translation move. The Hebrew word is *chug*, which means "circle" — a flat disc, a horizon line — not *kaddur*, which is the word for a ball or sphere (used in Isaiah 22:18). The standard critical commentaries — Brevard Childs in the OTL, Joseph Blenkinsopp in the Anchor Bible — all treat *chug* as describing a flat circular disc of land surrounded by waters, sitting under a domed firmament (*raqia*). That cosmology is everywhere in the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 1:6-8, Job 22:14, Job 38:13-14, Proverbs 8:27. It maps cleanly onto Mesopotamian flat-earth cosmology documented by Wayne Horowitz in *Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography*. So Isaiah 40:22 is not a spherical-earth verse. It is a flat-disc verse that some translations have made ambiguous in English. Now Matthew 4:8 — the temptation pericope. Davies and Allison in the ICC point out that the visual logic of "all the kingdoms of the world" being visible from a single mountain only makes sense in a worldview where the earth is flat enough that a high enough vantage point would show everything. Ulrich Luz in the Hermeneia volume agrees. The harmonization that the devil showed Jesus a vision is exactly the kind of post-hoc rationalization that has to be invented because the plain text doesn't work on a globe. The mountain in Matthew is a real mountain doing real geometry, and the geometry assumes a flat earth. Take your pick: either Isaiah 40:22 doesn't mean what apologists want it to mean, or Matthew 4:8 contradicts a sphere — most likely both.

answers.answer_explanation: [It is] he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof [are] as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in: (Isaiah 40:22)

answers.answer: All kingdoms can be seen from a high mountain, implying a flat earth
answers.answer_explanation: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; (Matthew 4:8)

commentary_out.commentary:
The entry pairs two distinct claims, and the apologetic case for biblical foreknowledge rests almost entirely on a single Hebrew word in Isaiah 40:22: "It is he that sitteth upon the circle (*chug*) of the earth." *Chug* denotes a circle, a horizon, a circumscribed disc — it is cognate with the verb meaning to draw a boundary or describe a compass arc, as in Job 26:10 ("he hath compassed the waters with bounds") and Proverbs 8:27 ("when he set a compass [*chug*] upon the face of the depth"). Biblical Hebrew possessed a separate word for a ball or sphere, *kaddur*, used in Isaiah 22:18 ("he will...toss thee like a ball [*kaddur*] into a large country"). The author of Isaiah 40 did not use it. A circle is a two-dimensional figure; a sphere is three-dimensional. Brevard Childs and Joseph Blenkinsopp both read *chug ha-arets* as the flat circular disc of inhabited land, surrounded by sea and capped by the heavens stretched "as a curtain" and "as a tent" — imagery in the same verse that presupposes a solid sky-dome, the *raqia* of Genesis 1:6-8.

This flat-disc cosmology is not idiosyncratic to Isaiah; it is the standard three-tier model of the Hebrew Bible and its Mesopotamian environment. The firmament is a beaten dome (Genesis 1; Job 37:18, where the skies are "strong, and as a molten looking glass"); the earth rests on pillars or foundations (1 Samuel 2:8; Psalm 104:5); waters lie above the dome and beneath the disc (Genesis 1:7; Psalm 148:4). Wayne Horowitz documents the close parallels in Mesopotamian cosmic geography, and Paul Seely's studies of the "firmament" and of the "earth and seas" demonstrate that ancient readers understood these terms concretely, not as veiled references to a globe. Isaiah 40:22, in short, is a flat-earth verse that certain English renderings have left ambiguous; it provides no evidence that the text knew the earth was spherical.

Matthew 4:8 supplies the second prong: the devil takes Jesus "up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them." Davies and Allison and Ulrich Luz both discuss whether the showing is literal-optical or visionary, and Davies-Allison observe that the tradition has affinities with apocalyptic mountain-vantage scenes (cf. the high mountain of Ezekiel 40:2 and the wilderness lookout of Deuteronomy 34:1-4) — neither commentator frames the verse as an explicit cosmological assertion that the earth is flat, so the flat-earth inference here is mine, drawn from the spatial logic of the passage rather than handed to me by the commentators. And that logic is straightforward: sufficient altitude affords a view of every kingdom on earth only on a worldview where a high vantage commands the whole disc. The strongest harmonization is that the showing was visionary or supernatural rather than optical: the devil presented the kingdoms in a panoramic vision (Luke 4:5 adds "in a moment of time," which some take to support a non-optical display), so no real line of sight is required and the geometry of a globe is irrelevant. This reading is not baseless; Luke's "in a moment of time" does push toward a preternatural showing. But Matthew, unlike Luke, anchors the scene to a literal "exceeding high mountain," the same evangelist who elsewhere uses mountains as concrete topographical settings (Matthew 5:1; 17:1; 28:16). The mention of the mountain's height is gratuitous on a purely visionary reading — height matters only if elevation aids sight. The most economical reading is that the tradition assumed the cosmology of its time. Either way the apologetic dilemma stands: Isaiah 40:22 does not teach a spherical earth, and Matthew 4:8 most naturally presupposes a flat one. Verdict: the foreknowledge claim is a translation artifact; the flat-earth reading of Matthew 4:8 is harmonizable as vision but is not the more natural sense.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The entry bundles two unequal prongs, and the single 'disputed' label tracks only the weaker half. The Isaiah 40:22 'sphere' claim does not survive the Hebrew at all: chug = circle/disc, not kaddur = ball, so that prong is effectively refuted rather than merely disputed. The genuine dispute is confined to Matthew 4:8, which can be read as a visionary, non-optical showing (Luke 4:5, 'in a moment of time'), neutralizing any geometric argument from a globe; against that, Matthew's emphasis on a literal 'exceeding high mountain' makes the flat-earth presupposition the more natural reading. Net: Isaiah refuted, Matthew disputed.

entries.question: Does God give freely or withhold his blessings?
entries.summary: James 1:5 and Luke 11:10 present God as giving freely and liberally to all who ask. But John 12:40 (quoting Isaiah 6:10) has God blinding eyes and hardening hearts so people cannot be converted; Joshua 11:20 says it was "of the LORD to harden their hearts" so they would fight Israel and be destroyed; and Isaiah 63:17 has the prophet accusing God of making his people "err from thy ways" and hardening their hearts. The contradiction is between God-as-generous-giver and God-as-active-spoiler-of-salvation.
entries.commentary: This is the Calvinist-Arminian fault line written into the canon itself. Apologists usually run two harmonizations. The first is the theodicy move — God hardens hearts only after the recipients have already hardened their own (cf. Romans 9:18 with the Pharaoh narrative as the test case). On this reading, divine hardening is judicial: God ratifies a prior human choice. Walter Brueggemann in the OTL Isaiah 40-66 commentary, and Douglas Moo in the NICNT Romans, both engage this seriously. The problem is that the texts don't actually support the "prior hardening" sequence consistently. Joshua 11:20 has the Canaanites hardened *so that* God can destroy them — the purpose is annihilation, and there's no indication of prior moral choice driving the divine action. Isaiah 63:17 has the prophet accusing God directly: "Why hast thou made us to err?" — this is not a recipient who hardened first. John 12:40, quoting Isaiah 6:10, makes the hardening the cause, not the consequence, of the people's failure to believe — the verse explicitly says God blinded and hardened them "that they should not see... and be converted, and I should heal them." The second harmonization, the Calvinist one, just bites the bullet: God sovereignly chooses to give to some and harden others, and James 1:5 applies only to the elect. This preserves consistency at the cost of making "giveth to all liberally" mean "giveth to the elect liberally," which is a meaningful narrowing the text doesn't perform on its own. So the apologist is stuck: either God's generosity is genuinely universal (in which case the hardening texts contradict it) or it's restricted (in which case James and Luke are speaking imprecisely). The contradiction is real and it runs through the canon's competing soteriologies.

answers.answer: God gives freely to those who ask
answers.answer_explanation:
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all [men] liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.

For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

answers.answer: God withholds his blessings and prevents men from receiving them
answers.answer_explanation:
He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with [their] eyes, nor understand with [their] heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly, [and] that they might have no favour, but that he might destroy them, as the LORD commanded Moses.

O LORD, why hast thou made us to err from thy ways, [and] hardened our heart from thy fear? Return for thy servants' sake, the tribes of thine inheritance.

commentary_out.commentary:
This entry sits on the Calvinist-Arminian fault line, but the underlying tension is older than that debate and is written into the canon itself. On one side stands a cluster of texts presenting God as an unstinting giver: James 1:5 promises that God "giveth to all liberally, and upbraideth not" (Greek *haplos*, "without reservation" or "singlemindedly," and *me oneidizontos*, "without reproach"), and Luke 11:10 universalizes the promise with *pas*, "everyone" who asks receives. On the other side stands a cluster of hardening texts in which God actively forecloses the very response he elsewhere invites.

The apologetic literature runs two harmonizations. The first is the judicial-hardening theodicy: God hardens only those who have already hardened themselves, so divine hardening ratifies a prior human choice. The Pharaoh narrative is the standard test case, since Exodus alternates between Pharaoh hardening his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 8:32, 9:34) and the LORD hardening it (Exodus 9:12, 10:1, 10:20), and Paul invokes it in Romans 9:18 ("whom he will he hardeneth"). Douglas Moo in the NICNT Romans treats this seriously, as does Walter Brueggemann on Isaiah. The difficulty is that the three OT/Johannine texts adduced here do not consistently encode the "prior hardening" sequence. Joshua 11:20 states that the Canaanites' hearts were hardened *so that* (Hebrew *lemaan*) they would engage Israel and be exterminated "that they might have no favour"; the stated purpose is annihilation, with no prior moral provocation in view. Isaiah 63:17 is more pointed still: the prophet, in a communal lament, accuses God directly — "Why hast thou made us to err (Hebrew *tatenu*) from thy ways, and hardened our heart from thy fear?" This is not a recipient who hardened first; it is an indictment of God as the cause, framed as a complaint and a plea for return.

John 12:40 is the decisive case. It cites Isaiah 6:10, and the textual form matters. The Masoretic Hebrew of Isaiah 6:10 is an imperative addressed to the prophet ("make the heart of this people fat"); the Septuagint shifts to a perfect describing the people's condition ("the heart of this people has grown dull"); John's wording diverges from both, casting God as the explicit agent: "He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart, that they should not see... and be converted, and I should heal them." The *hina* clause makes the divine blinding the cause, not the consequence, of unbelief, and the Evangelist immediately grounds Israel's rejection of Jesus in this hardening. Craig Keener and the standard Johannine commentaries note that John intensifies the agency of God beyond either the Hebrew or the Greek Vorlage.

The second harmonization is the Calvinist one, which simply bites the bullet: God sovereignly gives to the elect and hardens the reprobate, so James 1:5 and Luke 11:10 apply to those whom God has chosen to draw. This preserves logical consistency, but at the cost of reading "giveth to all liberally" as "giveth to the elect liberally" — a narrowing the text does not perform on its own. Scot McKnight's reading of James locates 1:5 within a wisdom-petition frame addressed to the believing community, which softens but does not eliminate the universalizing force of *pasin*, "to all."

The apologist is therefore caught between two horns. If God's generosity is genuinely universal, the hardening texts contradict it. If it is restricted to the elect, then James and Luke are speaking imprecisely and must be silently qualified. The tension is not a translation artifact or a misread context; it reflects genuinely competing soteriological currents — a Deuteronomistic and prophetic theology of divine hardening as judgment, and a wisdom-and-Gospel theology of God as open-handed giver — that the canon never reconciles at the level of doctrine. Verdict: genuine theological contradiction across competing canonical soteriologies.

entries.question: Can God's attributes be known?
entries.summary: Paul in Romans 1:20 says God's invisible attributes — his eternal power and divine nature — are "clearly seen" from the creation, so that humans are "without excuse." Job 11:7 has Zophar asking "Canst thou by searching find out God? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" — the implied answer being no. Isaiah 40:28 says of God "there is no searching of his understanding." The contradiction is between Paul's claim that God's nature is plainly accessible through observation of creation and the wisdom-tradition claim that God is fundamentally beyond human search.
entries.commentary: This one softens significantly once you parse what each text is actually claiming. Paul in Romans 1:20 is making a specific argument about *general revelation* — the existence of God and his power are evident from creation, which is enough to render Gentiles morally culpable. He's not claiming that the full divine nature is exhaustively knowable. Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Romans points out that Paul's argument has a polemical purpose: stripping Gentiles of the excuse of ignorance. Job 11:7 and Isaiah 40:28 are making a different claim — that God's *full* nature, his unsearchable understanding, his perfect knowability, exceeds human capacity. Both could be true at once: God's existence and power are evident, but his complete nature is unsearchable. Most apologists run this distinction and most critical scholars accept it. So the surface contradiction has a real exegetical resolution. The remaining problem is that Romans 1:20 has been historically deployed by apologists as much more than a minimal-knowability claim — it's used to argue that natural theology can deliver substantive attributes of God (omniscience, omnipotence, eternality, moral character) directly from observation of nature. That stronger reading does conflict with Job and Isaiah. So the contradiction is real if Romans 1:20 is read maximally and dissolves if it's read minimally. The standard exegesis goes minimal. The popular apologetic deployment goes maximal. That is of course a subjective call about the use rather than the text — but as a textual contradiction this entry is weaker than it looks. The verses can be reconciled by carefully delimiting what "knowing God" means in each context.

answers.answer: God's attributes are revealed in his works'
answers.answer_explanation: For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, [even] his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:

Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?

Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, [that] the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? [there is] no searching of his understanding.

commentary_out.commentary:
This tension softens considerably once each text's actual claim is parsed, and on the standard exegesis it dissolves into a familiar theological distinction rather than a contradiction.

Paul's statement in Romans 1:20 is a carefully bounded claim about general revelation. The Greek specifies what is perceptible: *ta aorata autou*, "his invisible attributes," further defined as *he aidios autou dynamis kai theiotes*, "his eternal power and divinity." These are "clearly seen" (*kathoratai*) and "understood" (*nooumena*) through the created order, with the explicit forensic purpose that humans be *anapologetous*, "without excuse." Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Romans and James Dunn in the WBC both stress the polemical function: Paul is constructing a courtroom indictment of Gentile humanity, depriving it of the plea of ignorance regarding God's existence and power. He is not asserting that the divine essence is exhaustively or perfectly knowable. There is a long-running lexical debate here, but it cuts both ways. A classic line of interpreters — R. C. Trench in his *Synonyms of the New Testament*, followed by C. E. B. Cranfield in the ICC — distinguishes *theiotes* (Rom 1:20: "divinity," the quality of being divine) from *theotes* (Col 2:9: "deity," the fullness of the Godhead). But this is contested, not settled: BDAG and a number of commentators treat the two words as effectively synonymous and caution against pressing the distinction, so it overstates the case to read a firm narrowing as Paul's certain intent. The distinction also lives entirely in the Greek — the KJV renders *both* terms "Godhead," so an English-only reader sees no contrast. The point that survives the debate is the modest one: Paul names eternal power and divinity in service of culpability, and nothing in the verse claims that creation yields an exhaustive account of God.

The Wisdom-tradition texts make a different claim. Job 11:7, on the lips of Zophar, asks "Canst thou by searching find out God? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" — the operative term being *ad-taklit*, "to the limit" or "to perfection," i.e., exhaustively. David Clines notes that the rhetorical question denies comprehensive knowledge, not the existence of any knowledge of God. Isaiah 40:28 declares "there is no searching (Hebrew *en heqer*) of his understanding" — a statement about the unfathomable depth of divine wisdom, set within a disputation meant to assure exiles that the Creator's purposes exceed their grasp. Joseph Blenkinsopp reads it as consolation grounded in transcendence, not as a denial that God can be known at all.

So the two clusters operate at different scopes. Romans 1:20 affirms minimal, propositional knowledge of God's existence and power from creation; Job and Isaiah deny exhaustive comprehension of God's full nature and understanding. Both can be true simultaneously: that God is, and is powerful, may be evident, while what God is, in the totality of his being, remains unsearchable. This is the classic distinction between knowability of existence and incomprehensibility of essence, and most apologists and most critical scholars alike accept it.

The residual tension is not textual but a matter of deployment. Romans 1:20 has frequently been pressed into service for a robust natural theology that claims to derive substantive divine attributes — omniscience, omnipotence, eternality, even moral character — directly from observing nature. That maximal reading does collide with Job 11:7 and Isaiah 40:28, which deny precisely such exhaustive access. But the maximal reading exceeds what Paul's own words assert; he names only eternal power and divinity, in service of culpability. When Romans 1:20 is read as Paul wrote it — minimally, forensically — there is no contradiction with the Wisdom tradition's insistence on incomprehensibility.

This entry is therefore weaker than it first appears. The verses can be reconciled by delimiting what "knowing God" means in each context, and that delimitation follows the grammar and rhetorical purpose of each passage rather than being imposed artificially. Verdict: overstated; harmonizable through the standard distinction between general revelation of God's existence/power and the incomprehensibility of his full essence.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The texts make different claims under different scopes: Romans 1:20 asserts that God's existence, eternal power, and divinity are evident from creation (general revelation rendering Gentiles culpable), while Job 11:7 and Isaiah 40:28 deny that God's full nature and unsearchable understanding can be exhaustively comprehended. Minimal knowability and incomprehensibility of the whole are jointly consistent.

entries.question: How long should David's throne endure?
entries.summary: Psalm 89:35-37 records God's oath, sworn by his holiness, that David's seed shall endure forever and his throne be established as the sun and moon — a faithful witness in heaven. Eight verses later, the same psalm — Psalm 89:44 — says God has "made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground." The contradiction is internal to a single psalm: the eternal oath in v. 35-37 is followed by the report of the throne's destruction in v. 44.
entries.commentary: Psalm 89 is one of the most theologically explosive texts in the entire Psalter, precisely because the contradiction is internal and intentional. The psalm is a three-part composition. Verses 1-37 rehearse the Davidic covenant in maximalist terms, climaxing in God's unbreakable oath. Verses 38-45 then describe the catastrophic reversal — God has rejected, abhorred, broken, profaned, cast down. Verses 46-51 are the lament's prayer for restoration. The psalm is not contradicting itself by accident. The psalmist is *holding God accountable* for the contradiction. The structure is: here is what you swore; here is what has happened; how long, O Lord. Most critical scholars (Tate, Hossfeld-Zenger, Goldingay) date the psalm's final form to the exilic or early post-exilic period, when the Davidic dynasty had been destroyed and the eternal covenant looked like a broken promise. The psalm preserves the older Davidic theology in vv. 1-37 (likely pre-exilic court material) and then juxtaposes it with the exilic reality in vv. 38-45 to confront God with the breach. Apologists harmonize by appealing to messianic fulfillment — the throne was "cast down" for Israel but "restored" in Christ, the eternal Davidic king. That's the standard New Testament reading (Acts 2:30, Hebrews 1:8), but it's a theological resolution to a textual problem that the psalmist himself does not resolve. The psalm ends in unanswered lament. The contradiction is not just real — it's *deliberate*, used as rhetorical pressure on Yahweh. Treating it as a problem to be harmonized away misses the psalm's own theological move.

answers.answer: David's throne was to endure forever
answers.answer_explanation:
Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David.

His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me.

It shall be established for ever as the moon, and [as] a faithful witness in heaven. Selah.
Thou hast made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground.

commentary_out.commentary:
Psalm 89 is among the most theologically charged compositions in the Psalter precisely because its self-contradiction is deliberate and structurally engineered. The psalm (a *maskil* attributed in its superscription to Ethan the Ezrahite) divides into three movements. Verses 1-37 rehearse the Davidic covenant in its most expansive form, drawing on the Nathan oracle of 2 Samuel 7 and reaching a climax in God's irrevocable oath: "Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David. His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me. It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven" (vv. 35-37). The oath is sworn *bi-qodshi*, "by my holiness," the strongest possible divine guarantee, and the comparison to the cosmic permanence of sun and moon makes the dynasty's perpetuity a fixture of the created order.

Verses 38-45 then execute an abrupt and devastating reversal. The same God who swore the oath has "cast off and abhorred," "made void the covenant," "profaned his crown," broken down his hedges, and — in v. 44 — "made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground." The vocabulary deliberately inverts the promises: the throne sworn to stand "as the sun" is hurled to the earth. Verses 46-51 turn to lament and petition — "How long, LORD? wilt thou hide thyself for ever?" — and the psalm ends without resolution, on an unanswered question and a closing doxology (v. 52) that belongs to the editorial seam closing Book III of the Psalter rather than to the psalm's own argument.

The juxtaposition is not a redactional accident or a careless contradiction. It is the psalm's central rhetorical instrument. The poet sets the maximal oath against the catastrophic reality in order to *confront God with the breach of covenant* — the logic is forensic: "This is what you swore; this is what has happened; how can both stand?" The contradiction is the complaint. To harmonize it away is to dismantle the very mechanism by which the lament does its theological work.

Critical scholarship (Tate, Hossfeld-Zenger, Goldingay) reads the final form as exilic or early post-exilic, composed after the fall of the Davidic monarchy in 587 BCE, when the "everlasting" dynasty had visibly ended. The pre-exilic court theology preserved in vv. 1-37 — itself drawing on the ancient Near Eastern royal-grant covenant type, in which a deity guarantees a dynasty perpetually — is set against the lived disaster of vv. 38-45 to dramatize the apparent failure of the divine word. Mowinckel situated the royal psalmody in cultic enthronement settings; whatever its earlier liturgical use, the present composition reframes that royal ideology as the premise of an unresolved theodicy.

The standard harmonization is messianic and Christian: the throne was "cast down" temporarily for historical Israel but "restored" eschatologically in Christ, the eternal Davidic king. The New Testament makes exactly this move — Acts 2:30 has Peter cite the Davidic oath as fulfilled in the resurrection, and Hebrews 1:8 applies enthronement language to the Son. This is a coherent later theological resolution, but it is imported from outside the psalm; Psalm 89 itself offers no such resolution. Its final word is interrogative — the covenant promise and the historical catastrophe are left in unrelieved collision, which is the poet's intent. Reading the messianic answer back into the psalm satisfies a canonical-theological harmony but does not remove the deliberate contradiction the psalmist constructed. Verdict: genuine and intentional contradiction, deployed as a rhetorical device of lament; resolved only by later messianic reinterpretation external to the psalm itself.

issues.problem: Citation #6 attributes a discussion of Psalm 89 ('on the literary movement of the psalm', bible_refs 'Psalms 89:44') to Nahum M. Sarna, On the Book of Psalms: Exploring the Prayers of Ancient Israel (Schocken, 1993), pp. 152-160. This is a misattribution. Sarna's book is not a full Psalms commentary; it gives chapter-length treatments of only ten selected psalms (Pss 1, 8, 15, 19, 24, 30, 48, 82, 93, 94). Psalm 89 is not among them and is not discussed in the volume, so neither the cited pages nor the attributed content (a treatment of Ps 89's literary movement) can be verified — they appear fabricated. The book itself is real (Schocken; ~312 pp.), but it does not cover Psalm 89.
issues.correction: Remove the Sarna citation (it does not treat Psalm 89), or replace it with a source that actually discusses Ps 89's literary structure (e.g., Tate WBC 20, Hossfeld-Zenger Hermeneia, or Goldingay BCOTWP, all already cited). The commentary body does not depend on Sarna, so removal is the cleanest fix.
